Then, cleaved ATF6 (cATF6) subsequently translocated to the nucleus and upregulated the expression of HSP90, which acts as a positive regulator of IFN regulatory factor 1 (IRF-1), thereby promoting the formation of the RIPK1 PANoptosome in TECs. Importantly, both the silencing of Rhbdf2 using neutrophil membrane-enveloped nanoparticles and the pharmacological inhibition of iRhom2 with sulforaphane alleviated renal damage in AKI model mice. Collectively, these results reveal iRhom2 as a key regulator of PANoptosis and suggest that targeting iRhom2 may represent a potential therapeutic strategy for AKI.

title: Gambogenic acid globally regulates translational processes in Nrf2-mutant esophageal squamous cell carcinoma by promoting Nrf2/MafG protein multimerization
abstract: Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) is a highly aggressive malignancy with limited therapeutic options and a high incidence in East Asia. Gain-of-function mutations in nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) are a major driver of ESCC progression, however, pharmacological interventions capable of effectively suppressing mutant Nrf2 signaling are currently lacking. Here, we conducted a high-throughput screen of 2141 natural products using Nrf2 reporter assays, fluorescence polarization, and Nrf2-dependent assays, and identified gambogenic acid (GNA) as a Nrf2-targeted inhibitor that preferentially attenuates oncogenic signaling driven by Nrf2 gain-of-function mutations in ESCC. GNA exhibited preferential anti-tumor activity in Nrf2-mutant ESCC cells compared with wild-type controls, both in vitro and in vivo. GNA also enhanced the chemosensitivity of Nrf2-mutant ESCC to cisplatin. Mechanistically, GNA suppressed the expression of Nrf2-driven ARE genes and modulated amino acid metabolism and mRNA translation by promoting cysteine oxidation in translational regulatory proteins within Nrf2-mutant cells. Importantly, GNA induced polymerization of the Nrf2/MafG protein complex and promoted its ubiquitin-mediated proteasomal degradation, thereby uncovering a previously uncharacterized mechanism of inhibition targeting the Nrf2/MafG axis. Collectively, our study identifies GNA as a promising therapeutic candidate that preferentially suppresses mutant Nrf2 signaling and shows therapeutic potential in Nrf2-driven ESCC.

title: Protein kinase WEE1 promotes cardiomyocytes ferroptosis and cardiac hypertrophy via the NF-κB/LCN2 axis
abstract: Under conditions of chronic pressure overload, cardiac hypertrophy can progressively develop into arrhythmias and heart failure, and in severe cases, may lead to sudden death. Previous studies have indicated that protein kinases play significant roles in cardiovascular diseases. This study aims to elucidate the function of the WEE1 G 2 checkpoint kinase (WEE1) in the progression of myocardial hypertrophy. We evaluated the expression of WEE1 in the hearts of mice with transverse aortic constriction (TAC). The functional role of WEE1 was investigated using siWEE1 in an angiotensin II (Ang II)-induced cardiomyocyte hypertrophy model. Furthermore, the contribution of WEE1 to cardiac hypertrophy was assessed in TAC mice via intraperitoneal administration of Adavosertib (WEE1-specific inhibitor). RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) was employed to identify the downstream effector molecules of WEE1 in cardiomyocytes. The expression of both phosphorylated WEE1 and WEE1 was upregulated in hearts subjected to transverse aortic constriction and in cardiac cells treated with angiotensin II. Knockdown of WEE1 effectively alleviated Ang II-induced cardiac cell hypertrophy. Furthermore, application of the specific inhibitor Adavosertib significantly attenuated cardiac cell hypertrophy and improved cardiac function. Mechanistic studies revealed that WEE1 promotes the translocation of the transcription factor P65 from the cytoplasm to the nucleus, thereby activating the nuclear factor κB (NF-κB) signaling pathway, which ultimately upregulates the transcriptional level of Lipocalin2 (LCN2). LCN2 mediates the process of ferroptosis in cardiac cells by binding to the ferroptosis receptor solute carrier family 22 member 17 (SLC22A17), thereby inducing cardiac hypertrophy. Our findings indicate that WEE1 exacerbates cardiac hypertrophy by activating the NF-κB signaling pathway, which upregulates LCN2 expression and subsequently aggravates ferroptosis in cardiac cells. Inhibition of WEE1 significantly improves cardiac function, highlighting its potential value as a therapeutic target of cardiac hypertrophy.

title: Targeting mitochondrial morphofunctional homeostasis and oxidative stress: Iristectorigenin A protects against cardiac remodeling via SIRT6/FOXO1 signaling
abstract: Myocardial remodeling, an essential pathological development in cardiovascular disease, is largely determined by disruptions in redox homeostasis and mitochondrial bioenergetic function. Iristectorigenin A (ITG), a naturally occurring isoflavone, exhibits a variety of pharmacological effects, including antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities. While so many protective effects, its specific effect on cardiac remodeling has not been reported previously. In this study, we aims to investigate the role of ITG in pressure overload-induced cardiac remodeling with a particular focus on mitochondrial function and oxidative stress. We revealed that ITG mitigated TAC-induced cardiac remodeling and improved cardiac function, with the 20 mg/kg dose showing optimal efficacy; further escalation to 40 mg/kg provided no additional benefit. ITG attenuated cardiomyocyte hypertrophy and inhibited activation of fibroblasts in vitro. Additionally, ITG treatment effectively suppressed oxidative stress and inflammation in the hearts of TAC mice, while improving mitochondrial morphology and the integrity of inner membrane structure. Notably, surface plasmon resonance (SPR) analysis indicated a direct interaction between SIRT6 and ITG with micromolar affinity. Besides, sustained TAC- or PE-stimulation impaired cardiac sirtuin 6 (SIRT6) protein levels, which were partially reversed by ITG. More importantly, silencing SIRT6 and SIRT6 knockdown separately inhibited the protective effects of ITG in vitro and in vivo. Mechanistically, ITG promotes SIRT6 levels by inhibiting its ubiquitination degradation. Furthermore, the cardioprotective effect of ITG was concomitant with SIRT6 upregulation, deacetylation and dephosphorylation of forkhead box protein O1 (FOXO1) and the subsequent increased transcription of antioxidant genes. Collectively, we firstly discover that ITG inhibits oxidative stress and safeguards mitochondrial morphofunctional homeostasis in response to pathological stress through activating SIRT6/FOXO1 axis, suggesting the therapeutic potential of ITG in the treatment of cardiac hypertrophy and remodeling, providing a promising avenue for future research and potential clinical application. Schematic illustration of ITG's potential protective mechanism against cardiac hypertrophy.

title: Loss of Tars induces proteostasis stress and drives HSPC exhaustion through mTORC1 activation
abstract: Hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) rely on tightly regulated proteostasis to preserve their self-renewal and differentiation potential throughout life. However, how proteostasis stress induced by translational dysregulation affects HSPC homeostasis remains poorly understood. Here, we found that knockout of the cytoplasmic threonyl-tRNA synthetase (Tars), which is a component of the translation machinery, caused HSPC exhaustion and definitive, but not primitive, hematopoiesis defects in zebrafish. Similarly, TARS functional deficiency resulted in human CD34 + HSC exhaustion and a decrease in colony-forming unit-granulocyte, macrophage (CFU-GM) and colony-forming unit-macrophage (CFU-M) numbers while sparing burst-forming unit-erythroid (BFU-E) numbers in vitro. Functional rescue experiments demonstrated that the enzymatic activity of Tars is indispensable for HSPC maintenance and definitive hematopoiesis. Interestingly, these phenotypes occurred prior to the apparent decrease in global protein translation and were independent of global translation inhibition, hinting that these defective HSPCs were eliminated by an unknown mechanism. Transcriptomic and proteomic profiling revealed that Tars deletion caused widespread proteomic reprogramming and mTORC1 signaling activation, whereas pharmacological or genetic inhibition of mTORC1 partially rescued HSPC exhaustion in tars -/- embryos. These findings uncover a link between translational machinery integrity, mTORC1 signaling, and HSPC fate determination, providing critical insight into how proteostasis stress is sensed and resolved to maintain hematopoietic homeostasis.

title: TINA: a geometry-aware post-hoc scoring framework for protein-protein interaction
abstract: Accurate identification of the most native-like conformation remains a critical bottleneck in protein complex structure prediction, particularly when multiple globally plausible candidate models are generated by deep learning methods such as AlphaFold3 (AF3). While AF3 provides internal confidence metrics such as ipTM and pLDDT, these signals often lack sufficient sensitivity to distinguish subtle but structurally meaningful differences in local interface geometry. Here, we present TINA, a geometry-aware post-hoc scoring framework designed for fine-grained ranking and selection among high-quality protein complex candidates. TINA constructs atom-level interface graphs and explicitly models two-body, three-body, and four-body geometric interactions through a many-body tensor modeling strategy, enabling a more comprehensive characterization of local contact patterns, angular arrangements, and torsional constraints. The model is initially trained using a joint ranking and regression objective on a large decoy set generated by ZDOCK, with additional task-specific fine-tuning for protein-peptide complexes, and is evaluated exclusively on AF3-generated candidate pools across four independent benchmarks covering general protein-protein, antibody-antigen, protein-peptide, and antibody-peptide complexes. TINA consistently achieves superior or competitive performance in terms of top-1 success rate, enrichment factor, and top-1 DockQ quality. Notably, its benefit is most pronounced in low-confidence and antibody-related scenarios, where AF3 internal ranking signals are less effective in discriminating among candidate conformations. Representative case studies demonstrate that TINA successfully identifies near-native conformations that are present in the AF3 decoy pool but overlooked by ipTM. Ablation experiments further confirm the critical contributions of atom-level graphs, many-body geometric modules, and the joint loss design. Overall, TINA demonstrates that independent, interface-focused post-hoc scoring remains a valuable complement to AF3, particularly for challenging complexes where local geometric discrimination is critical for accurate model selection.

title: FTO promotes human NK cell proliferation yet restricts effector functions
abstract: Human embryonic stem cell (hESC)- or induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived natural killer (NK) cells serve as promising adoptive cell therapies for cancer patients and as valuable models for studying the regulation of human NK cell development and effector functions. In this study, we used shRNA to knock down the expression of FTO in hESCs and differentiated these cells into NK cells to explore the role of FTO in regulating human NK cell development and effector functions. Our data revealed that the FTO knockdown in hESCs resulted in a comparable effect on haematopoietic progenitor cell generation but significantly impaired CD45⁺CD56⁺ NK cell production, which might be attributed to impaired proliferation, as indicated by reduced Ki-67 expression. Functional assays demonstrated that FTO knockdown in hESC-NK cells effectively increased per-cell cytotoxicity, including the expression of perforin, granzyme B, and IFN-γ, and increased degranulation (as indicated by the CD107a level). Integrated MeRIP-seq and RNA-seq analyses identified ADAMTS1 and ZAP70 as key target genes of FTO, demonstrating that FTO knockdown increased m⁶A methylation near the 3'UTR regions of ADAMTS1 and ZAP70 mRNAs and upregulated their transcript levels. ADAMTS1 is a known proliferation inhibitor, whereas increased ZAP70 expression is accompanied by increased phosphorylation of ERK1/2, a downstream component of ZAP70 signalling cascades, which positively regulates the effector functions of NK cells. Overall, our results demonstrate that FTO maintains human NK cell proliferation but restricts their per-cell effector functions, possibly through regulating the m⁶A methylation of ADAMTS1 and ZAP70 mRNAs. Exploring methods to achieve stage-specific FTO knockdown in mature NK cells may provide a potential strategy to optimize hESC-NK cell-based immunotherapy.

title: DYT8 drives lung adenocarcinoma through EGFR-mediated PSMC6 recruitment and uncharacterized phosphorylation at Ser 306 and 525 of c-Src
abstract: Lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) is a multi-kinase hyperactivation-driven malignancy. Targeted therapies are effective but have limited application, primarily due to a small eligible patient population and the development of drug resistance. Analysis of TCGA and tissue microarray show that Dystonia 8 (DYT8) is specially highly expressed in more than 70% of LUAD patients. Furthermore, increased DYT8 expression is positively associated with tumor malignancy and negatively associated with survival. Using the Dyt8 knock-in (cKras LSL-G12D/+ p53 R172H/+ -Dyt8-KI) and knockout (cKras LSL-G12D/+ p53 R172H/+ -Dyt8-KO) transgenic mice, we identify DYT8 as key activator that accelerates the initiation and progression of LUAD. Mechanistically, EGFR-mediated phosphorylation of DYT8 at Y120 reinforces its stability by increasing its interaction with PSMC6, a protein that is highly expressed in LUAD and associated with an unfavorable prognosis. DYT8 drives LUAD malignant transformation by activating Src. Although Y419 phosphorylation is a recognized key event in Src-driven LUAD, our study identifies novel phosphorylation sties at S306 and S525 that are activated by DYT8, which these novel sites being more critical for DYT8-driven malignant transformation than Y419 phosphorylation. Furthermore, the knockdown of Dyt8 rescues EGFR-triggered carcinogenesis and resistance to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (EGFR-TKIs). These findings reveal that DYT8 drives LUAD via a previously unreported Src activation mechanism and identify EGFR-DYT8-PSMC6 axis as the key determinant of high DYT8 level, thereby conferring a novel therapeutic strategy for wider LUAD patients, including those with EGFR-TKIs resistant.

title: MD2-IN-1 restores microglial lysosomal function and attenuates amyloid pathology through TREM2-associated signaling in 5×FAD mice
abstract: Triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 2 (TREM2) is a central regulator of microglial adaptation during Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet the development of small-molecule modulators associated with TREM2 signaling remains limited. Here, through a consensus pharmacophore-guided virtual screening strategy, MD2-IN-1 was identified as a candidate small molecule associated with TREM2 signaling. Biolayer interferometry and cellular thermal shift assays supported cellular target engagement related to TREM2 (K D = 13.85 μM). In Aβ-stimulated BV2 microglia, MD2-IN-1 increased SYK phosphorylation, promoted Aβ uptake, and shifted microglial responses toward a less proinflammatory phenotype. These effects were markedly attenuated following Trem2 knockdown, indicating the involvement of the TREM2-SYK signaling pathway. Mechanistically, MD2-IN-1 restored lysosomal acidification and increased the expression of the V-ATPase subunits ATP6v0c and ATP6v0a1, accompanied by increased intracellular Aβ degradation. In 5×FAD mice, chronic MD2-IN-1 administration improved cognitive performance without detectable behavioral abnormalities compared with WT animals. Multimodal PET imaging demonstrated reduced amyloid deposition and attenuated neuroinflammatory signals, which were further supported by histological analyses showing decreased plaque burden, reduced inflammatory microglial responses, and preserved neuronal integrity. In addition, MD2-IN-1 reduced P62 accumulation and restored ATP6v0c expression in vivo, whereas these effects were partially attenuated by pharmacological inhibition of TREM2. Collectively, these findings identify MD2-IN-1 as a small-molecule modulator associated with TREM2 signaling that restores microglial lysosomal degradative function and promotes Aβ clearance in AD models, providing pharmacological support for targeting adaptive microglial responses in AD.

title: Correction: Je-Chun-Jun induced apoptosis of human cervical carcinoma HeLa cells
Restoration of cyclin A2 by glabridin reverses pathological cell cycle arrest and drives cardiac repair in HFpEF
abstract: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is a pervasive clinical syndrome characterized by complex and elusive pathogenic mechanisms. In this study, we identify aberrant cardiomyocyte cell cycle arrest as a previously unrecognized pathological driver of HFpEF that hinders tissue repair. Using in vivo and in vitro models, we further demonstrate that Glabridin (Gla), a bioactive isoflavone, can induce cardiac repair and alleviate myocardial hypertrophy and fibrosis in HFpEF by targeting the cell cycle arrest pathway. Mechanistically, Gla exerts its protective effects by specifically inhibiting the degradation of Cyclin A2 (CCNA2) and mitigating cardiomyocyte oxidative damage. This stabilization of CCNA2 effectively abrogates cell cycle arrest and drives cardiomyocyte cell cycle re-entry, an effect that was successfully recapitulated by CCNA2 gain-of-function experiments. This reparative response is intrinsically coupled with the restoration of metabolic homeostasis and the attenuation of oxidative stress, as evidenced in both cardiac and hepatic cells. Collectively, our findings define cell cycle arrest as a novel target and position Gla as a potent inducer of CCNA2-mediated cardiac repair for HFpEF treatment.

title: Systematic optimization and characterization of the MidTAC platform for targeted protein degradation
abstract: Biological proteolysis-targeting chimeras (BioPROTACs), which employ peptide or protein-based targeting ligands to recruit endogenous degradation machinery, offer a promising strategy to expand the scope of targeted protein degradation. The recently discovered Midnolin employs a distinct, ubiquitin-independent "capture-degradation" mechanism that engages the proteasome directly, offering a complementary mechanistic strategy. However, the design principles, domain requirements, and substrate selectivity of Midnolin-based targeting chimeras (MidTAC) remain poorly understood. In this study, we systematically optimized the MidTAC platform and defined its functional boundaries. We demonstrated that optimal degradation activity requires the targeting module, the anti-GFP nanobody VHHGFP4 (variable domain of heavy chain of heavy-chain-only antibody against GFP variant 4), to be fused to the N-terminus of full-length Midnolin, as C-terminal or internal insertions are ineffective. Domain dissection revealed that neither the ubiquitin-like (UBL) domain nor the alpha-helical C-terminal (αHelix-C) domain alone, nor their simple tandem, is sufficient for degradation; the intact spatial conformation of the Midnolin scaffold is essential. Notably, MidTAC efficiently degraded substrate proteins irrespective of their subcellular localization, demonstrating its broad-spectrum utility. Furthermore, fusing the VHL E3 ligase to the C-terminus of Midnolin significantly enhanced degradation efficiency, suggesting a synergistic effect between ubiquitin-independent capture and ubiquitin-dependent recruitment. Collectively, these findings provide the first systematic characterization of MidTAC configuration, domain requirements, and broad-spectrum degradability, establishing a refined framework for engineering of next-generation BioPROTACs with an expanded substrate range.

title: MMP14-mediated proteolytic cleavage of LAMC2 domain III fragment drives osimertinib resistance in EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer
abstract: Acquired resistance to osimertinib remains a critical clinical challenge in EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), with 40%-60% of progressing patients lacking an identifiable genetic resistance driver. Through quantitative secretomic profiling of paired osimertinib-sensitive and -resistant NSCLC cell lines, we identified laminin subunit γ2 (LAMC2) as markedly enriched in resistant cell secretomes. Single-cell RNA sequencing reanalysis revealed a LAMC2-high drug-tolerant persister subpopulation that expanded under osimertinib pressure, with pseudotime analysis suggesting progressive co-upregulation of LAMC2 and matrix metalloproteinase 14 (MMP14) along the treatment-to-resistance trajectory. Across four independent cohorts, MMP14 exhibited the strongest co-expression with LAMC2 among all metalloproteinases; the two proteins also physically interacted, and their concurrent high expression predicted the worst overall survival. Mechanistically, MMP14 cleaved LAMC2 to release a bioactive Domain III (DIII) fragment harboring EGF-like repeats, which reactivated EGFR/AKT/ERK signaling despite continued osimertinib exposure. Exogenous DIII conferred resistance in sensitive cells, whereas an anti-DIII blocking antibody reversed MMP14-driven resistance in cell lines and patient-derived organoids. The selective MMP14 inhibitor NSC405020 restored osimertinib sensitivity in vitro and suppressed xenograft growth. In residual tumor tissues from neoadjuvant osimertinib-treated patients, non-responders exhibited higher LAMC2/MMP14 co-expression and more prominent spatial exclusion of CD8⁺ T-cells from the tumor core compared with major pathological responders. These findings identify the MMP14-LAMC2-DIII proteolytic axis as a non-genetic resistance mechanism and suggest that MMP14 inhibition or DIII neutralization may represent a rational strategy to overcome acquired osimertinib resistance.

title: Context-dependent vascular effects of platycodin D: inhibition of neointima formation but aggravation of atherosclerosis with involvement of mTORC1 signaling
abstract: Platycodin D (PD), a triterpenoid saponin from Platycodon grandiflorus, has been reported to have cardiovascular activity, but its actions in vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs) and atherosclerosis remain unclear. We integrated network pharmacology, molecular docking, 100-ns molecular dynamics simulation, VSMC assays, and two mouse carotid models. In VSMCs cultured under basal conditions, PD reduced viability and BrdU incorporation, downregulated cyclin D1/E1, and induced TUNEL positivity and cleaved caspase-3. At the cellular level, PD activated mTORC1-associated signaling, increased p70S6K and eIF2α phosphorylation, increased ATF4 protein and activated ATF6, impaired autophagic flux, and induced CHOP-associated endoplasmic reticulum stress. Rapamycin and 4-phenylbutyric acid attenuated PD-induced apoptosis, whereas MHY1485 and thapsigargin exacerbated it. Perivascular PD reduced neointimal hyperplasia after complete carotid ligation in C57BL/6J mice. In contrast, PD accelerated early carotid atherosclerosis after partial ligation in ApoE -/- mice fed a high-fat diet. Under ox-LDL challenge, PD increased VSMC lipid accumulation, Olr1/Cd36 expression, mTORC1-p70S6K signaling, and BrdU incorporation; rapamycin limited these effects. These findings suggest that PD activates an mTORC1-associated stress program whose vascular outcome depends on lipid and flow context. PD may have local anti-neointimal potential but warrants caution in hyperlipidemic atherosclerosis.

title: A novel shark VNAR antibody-based immunotoxin targeting ERα36 disrupts non-genomic estrogen signaling and tumor metabolic reprogramming in breast cancer
abstract: ERα36, a membrane-associated splice variant of estrogen receptor α, mediates rapid non-genomic estrogen signaling and is frequently overexpressed in aggressive and therapy-resistant breast cancers. Although ERα36 represents a promising therapeutic target, its clinical exploitation remains limited due to the lack of high-affinity and highly specific targeting ligands capable of recognizing its extracellular domain. In this paper, we constructed a shark-derived variable new antigen receptor (VNAR) phage display immune library and isolated two high-affinity VNAR single-domain antibodies (FR6 and TH4) targeting distinct epitopes on ERα36. The TH4 VNAR was further engineered by fusion with a truncated Pseudomonas aeruginosa exotoxin (PE24) to generate a recombinant immunotoxin (TH4-PE24), characterized by (1) high specificity and affinity for ERα36 (K D = 0.751 nmol/L), (2) potent and selective cytotoxicity against ERα36-positive breast cancer cells (IC 50 = 1.54 nmol/L), (3) a dual mechanism involving ERα36 degradation and suppression of PI3K/AKT and MAPK/ERK signaling pathways, and (4) significant in vivo antitumor efficacy in xenograft models without observable systemic toxicity. With this immunotoxin, we further investigated how ERα36 targeting could remodel tumor metabolism. ERα36-mediated metabolic regulation in breast cancer is a new research direction with many aspects unknown. We found that TH4-PE24 treatment led to extensive metabolic reprogramming, including disruption of nucleotide metabolism, ABC transporters, and central carbon metabolism. Overall, we report a novel shark VNAR-based immunotoxin platform that can achieve precise and potent antitumor effects by targeting the previously intractable membrane receptor ERα36. The modular design features make it translational for various other studies, such as targeting additional immune checkpoint molecules and developing next-generation precision therapeutics against membrane receptors that are inaccessible to conventional antibody modalities. The schematic diagram illustrates the screening of shark-derived variable new antigen receptors (VNARs) targeting estrogen receptor α, the identification and functional characterization of antigen-binding epitopes, and the construction of a VNAR-based immunotoxin, together with its in vitro and in vivo antitumor efficacy and safety evaluation. Estrogen receptor α36 (ERα36) is a membrane-associated splice variant of estrogen receptor α that primarily mediates non-genomic estrogen signaling. Owing to the α-helical structure of its C-terminal 27 amino acids, ERα36 has long been considered difficult to target with functionally active antibodies. Shark VNARs possess a unique and extended CDR3 region, enabling the recognition of complex and conformational epitopes. Taking advantage of this structural feature, we achieved functional targeting of ERα36 and identified two VNARs that recognize distinct linear and conformational epitopes, respectively. Among them, the conformational epitope-recognizing VNAR, TH4, was further employed to construct a novel immunotoxin. This immunotoxin not only suppresses ERα36 expression in breast cancer cells but also inhibits AKT and ERK signaling pathways, leading to reduced breast cancer cell proliferation and attenuation of tumorigenicity in ERα36-positive breast cancer.

title: Anticancer drug discovery: Embracing the next wave of innovation
Inhibition of histone deacetylase 3 alleviates lithocholic acid-induced intrahepatic cholestasis by enhancing expression of bile acid and lipid homeostasis-related genes
abstract: There is a lack of effective therapies for cholestatic liver injury. Recent studies have shown that pan-inhibitors of histone deacetylases (HDACs) play a protective role in cholestasis and fibrosis, but the dynamic changes and role of histone deacetylase 3 (HDAC3) under these conditions remain unclear. In the current study, the expression of acetylation-modifying enzymes, including HDAC3, in livers from lithocholic acid (LCA)-induced intrahepatic and bile duct ligation (BDL)-induced extrahepatic cholestatic mice, as well as in cholestatic patients, was examined. HDAC3 was aberrantly upregulated in the livers of cholestatic mice and patients. Functional studies in LCA- and BDL-induced cholestatic mouse models using RGFP966, a specific HDAC3 inhibitor, were then performed. Pharmacological inhibition of HDAC3 significantly alleviated liver injury in LCA-induced cholestasis but had no protective effect on BDL-induced cholestasis, as assessed by survival tests, gross examination, H&E staining, serum biochemical assays, cytokine expression, and immunohistochemical staining of immune cell biomarkers. Mechanistically, HDAC3 inhibition upregulated genes involved in bile acid and lipid homeostasis in LCA-induced cholestatic mice, as determined by RNA-Seq and validated by RT‒qPCR and Western blotting. The upregulation of these genes, together with increased levels of acetylation of histone H3 at lysine 9 (H3K9Ac) and lysine 27 (H3K27Ac), was validated in transformed human liver epithelial-2 (THLE-2) cells treated with RGFP966. In summary, this study demonstrated that HDAC3 is a potential therapeutic target for LCA-induced intrahepatic cholestasis, with inhibition exerting protective effects through genes involved in bile acid and lipid homeostasis, possibly via epigenetic regulation.

title: ASIC1a promotes liver fibrosis by inhibiting METTL3 SUMOylation
abstract: Liver fibrosis represents a major global health burden, with its core pathological feature being the excessive deposition of extracellular matrix driven by activated hepatic stellate cells (HSCs). Acid-sensitive ion channel 1a (ASIC1a) has been shown to be associated with the progression of liver fibrosis, but the molecular mechanisms by which it regulates RNA m 6 A methylation remain unclear. The aim of this study is to investigate the role of ASIC1a in liver fibrosis and the specific regulatory pathways involved. Experiments were conducted using human liver fibrosis tissue, a carbon tetrachloride-induced mouse model of liver fibrosis, and rat hepatic stellate cells; a mouse model with a hepatic stellate cell-specific ASIC1a knockout was generated; performed RIP-qPCR to validate METTL3 binding to target transcripts, while global m 6 A levels were assessed by dot blot and methyltransferase activity assays, the molecular mechanisms were elucidated using methods such as immunoprecipitation, mass spectrometry, SUMOylation assays, and quantitative m⁶A methylation analysis. ASIC1a is significantly up-regulated in fibrotic liver tissue and activated hepatic stellate cells; specific knockout of ASIC1a significantly reduces the severity of liver fibrosis in mice. Mechanistically, ASIC1a binds to SAE1 to inhibit the SUMOylation of METTL3, thereby enhancing its m 6 A methyltransferase activity, which in turn promotes the activation of hepatic stellate cells and the progression of fibrosis. This study has revealed a novel ASIC1a-METTL3-m 6 A de-SUMOylation regulatory axis in the progression of liver fibrosis, suggesting that ASIC1a may serve as a potential target for anti-fibrotic therapy.

title: Transcription factor EB as a novel target for dimethyl fumarate to restore endothelial function in diabetes
abstract: Diabetes mellitus-associated endothelial dysfunction represents a pivotal early event in diabetic vasculopathy, linking metabolic derangements to vascular injury. Dimethyl fumarate (DMF), an FDA-approved drug for multiple sclerosis and psoriasis, exhibits potent anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties, yet whether it protects against diabetic endothelial dysfunction and the underlying molecular mechanisms remain unclear. Here, diabetic db/db mice and the non-diabetic db/m + littermates were treated with DMF (100 mg·kg -1 ·d -1 ) or vehicle for 4 weeks, and vascular function in aortic and mesenteric artery rings was assessed by wire myography. Human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) and endothelial cell (EC)-specific Tfeb knockout ( Tfeb ECKO ) mice were employed to investigate the target of DMF in vitro and in vivo. DMF restored the impaired endothelium-dependent relaxations (EDRs) in db/db mouse aortas and insulin-induced relaxations in mesenteric arteries, improved glucose tolerance, reduced aortic endothelial mitochondrial ROS (mito-ROS) accumulation, and lowered the expression of inflammatory markers. IL-1β induced phosphorylation and cytoplasmic retention of TFEB (indicative of TFEB inhibition), mito-ROS production, and inflammatory responses in HUVECs and mouse aortas, all of which were reversed by DMF pretreatment. These protective effects of DMF were largely reversed by TFEB knockdown in HUVECs or in aortas of Tfeb ECKO mice. RNA sequencing data analysis revealed a substantial overlap between DMF-regulated and TFEB-overexpression transcriptional profiles, implicating a role of TFEB in DMF-induced suppression of inflammatory and oxidative pathways. Together, DMF ameliorates endothelial dysfunction in diabetes by inhibiting TFEB phosphorylation and restoring TFEB nuclear activity. Endothelial TFEB represents a critical mediator responsible for the vaso-protective effects of DMF and a promising therapeutic target for the treatment of diabetic vascular complications.

title: TNF signaling at the brain-heart interface: neurovascular injury and cardiovascular vulnerability in epilepsy
abstract: Epilepsy is increasingly viewed as a systemic disorder in which recurrent seizures intersect with vascular, autonomic, respiratory, and cardiac processes to influence cardiovascular vulnerability. Seizure-related neuroinflammation involves multiple interacting mediator pathways, including HMGB1/TLR4-RAGE signaling, inflammasome/IL-1β activation, IL-6/IL-6R-gp130 signaling, albumin/TGF-β signaling following blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption, and tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α)/TNF receptor (TNFR) signaling. Within this inflammatory network, TNF/TNFR signaling represents a mechanistically distinct and translationally relevant framework for examining how immune activation intersects with endothelial-barrier dysfunction, neurovascular unit injury, autonomic disturbance, inflammatory communication across neural and cardiovascular compartments, and cardiac vulnerability. This review integrates direct evidence from epilepsy studies with mechanistic insights from related experimental studies of BBB injury, myocardial ischemia-reperfusion injury, cardioprotection, and brain-heart communication. TNF biology is determined by ligand form, receptor subtype, cellular compartment, and disease context. Soluble TNF preferentially engages TNFR1-associated inflammatory and injury-amplifying pathways, whereas transmembrane TNF/TNFR2 signaling may support regulatory or reparative responses in selected settings. In epilepsy, seizure-associated inflammation, BBB dysfunction, glial activation, and autonomic imbalance may interact to increase susceptibility to arrhythmogenic stress, myocardial injury, adverse cardiac remodeling, and cardiorespiratory instability relevant to sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP). However, epilepsy-specific evidence directly linking TNF/TNFR signaling to cardiovascular outcomes remains limited, and many mechanistic connections currently rely on converging evidence from neurovascular and cardiovascular research. Future studies should integrate compartment-resolved inflammatory profiling with autonomic, respiratory, electrocardiographic, and cardiac phenotyping to distinguish inflammatory signatures of disease severity from modifiable contributors to cardiovascular risk. Such approaches may enable phenotype-specific strategies to better understand and ultimately mitigate the brain-heart consequences of epilepsy.

title: Aloperine induces methuosis in non-small cell lung cancer by targeting VPS34 lactylation and disrupting the Armus/Rab7 axis
abstract: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) represents the most prevalent form of malignant tumor and constitutes a principal cause of cancer-related mortality globally. Conventional therapeutic approaches predominantly induce apoptosis; however, their efficacy is often compromised by the development of drug resistance. Methuosis, a form of regulated cell death distinct from apoptosis, is characterized by aberrant macropinocytosis and the formation of cytoplasmic vacuoles. Aloperine (ALO), a naturally occurring antitumor alkaloid, has been observed to induce methuosis in cancer cells, although its precise molecular targets and mechanisms remain to be elucidated. This study investigated the anti-NSCLC effects of ALO using cell lines, patient-derived organoids, and mouse xenograft models. Through various assays, it was demonstrated that ALO directly interacts with VPS34 at the I760 residue and promotes TIP60-mediated lactylation of VPS34 at K356 and K781. This interaction inhibits VPS34 kinase activity and reduces intracellular PI(3)P production. The subsequent decrease in PI(3)P levels impedes Armus endosomal recruitment, disrupts Rab7 cycling, leads to the accumulation of macropinosomes, and impairs endolysosomal fusion, ultimately inducing methuosis. ALO exhibits significant antitumor efficacy and acts synergistically with cisplatin to co-activate methuosis and apoptosis, all while avoiding noticeable systemic toxicity. Collectively, ALO targets VPS34 lactylation and disrupts Armus/Rab7 signaling. When used in conjunction with cisplatin, it constitutes a safe and effective therapeutic strategy for NSCLC.
